How to scan a QR code from an image or screenshot

You can scan a QR code even when you cannot point a phone at it, for example when it is in an email, a PDF or a screenshot.

  1. Save or screenshot the image that contains the QR code.
  2. Click Choose image above, or drag the picture onto the box. You can also paste a screenshot with Ctrl+V (Cmd+V on Mac).
  3. The tool reads the code and shows what is inside: the link, WiFi details, contact card or plain text.
  4. Check the result. For links, look at the domain first and only then open it.

If nothing is found, crop the image closer to the code, use a sharper picture, or add a white border around the code.

Scanning with a camera

On a phone, the built-in camera app reads QR codes on current iPhones and most Android phones, so you may not need this tool. If you want to see the content before opening it, or you are on a laptop with a webcam, press Use camera and allow camera access when asked. The camera needs a secure (https) page.

Your camera image is processed on your device and is not uploaded or stored.

What a QR code can contain

A QR code is only a container for text. What happens next depends on what the text says. This scanner recognises the common kinds and explains them.

ContentWhat you see hereWhat a phone would do
Web linkThe full address and its domainOpen the website
WiFi networkNetwork name, security type and passwordOffer to join the network
Contact card (vCard)Name, company, phone and emailOffer to save the contact
UPI payment requestPayee, UPI ID and amountOpen a payment app
Email, phone, SMSThe address or numberStart the email, call or message
Plain textThe text itselfShow the text

How to check a QR code before you open it

Scam QR codes exist, for example stickers placed over real ones or codes in unsolicited mail. Reading the content first is the safest habit.

  • Look at the domain. Does it match the company you expect? Watch for spelling tricks and unusual endings.
  • Be careful with payment requests. Scanning to receive money does not exist. If a code asks you to pay, check the payee and amount.
  • Distrust urgency. Codes that promise prizes, refunds or demand quick action are a red flag.
  • Check physical stickers. If a code on a parking meter or poster looks stuck on top of another, do not use it.
  • Avoid entering passwords on a page you reached only through a QR code, unless you trust the site.

Why won't my QR code scan?

Most failures have a simple cause.

  • The image is too small or blurry. Use the original file or a higher-resolution screenshot.
  • No white border. QR codes need blank space around them. Add a margin or crop less tightly.
  • Low contrast or inverted colors. Light-on-dark codes and pale colors are harder to read.
  • The code is damaged or too dense. Long content creates a complex pattern. Ask the sender for a simpler code.
  • It is not a QR code. Barcodes and data matrix codes need a different scanner.

Made the code yourself? Use the QR code tester to see if it will scan when printed small.
